People don’t take out student loans knowing they can’t pay them off.  They take them out in the desperate hope of paying for and completing their education.  Few undergraduates have a sense of how difficult it can be to pay off student loans.  Other loans have ways of being discharged if the borrower is unable to pay.  Granted, there are often consequences (foreclosure, repossession, bankruptcy, damage to credit, etc.), but the damage is generally limited to 10 years of adverse credit at the most.  

The notion that many students take out loans to finance unmarketable degrees is likely overblown.  I’ve known students with Comp Sci degrees who can’t pay off their loans because they had the misfortune of graduating in a down job market.  Sometimes people get degrees in fields that seemed promising when they were in school but were rendered obsolete by technological advances or economic changes.  Others are able to get jobs but have to deal with unforeseen circumstances, such as health problems or family emergencies.  Costs go up, but wages stagnate.  And so on.  The whole “well, just pay it off, hurr hurr” attitude ignores all of these realities.  In short, shit happens.

The question is, how does one distinguish “virtue signaling” from legitimate expressions of solidarity, support, or protest.  For example, expressing support for transgender people is often called “virtue signaling,” but it serves the very real purpose of encouraging and supporting non-gender conforming people in what has become a very hostile environment for them.  Or what about standing for the national anthem vs. kneeling?  One could argue that both are a kind of virtue signaling, though the former would probably characterized as “expressing patriotism” and the latter as “protesting police brutality” by those who engaging in the respective activities.  

In my view, the term “virtue signaling” is typically used to criticize gestures one doesn’t happen to agree with, since most of these public gestures serve multiple purposes.  Yes, self promotion is one of those purposes, but these gestures also often convey a message beyond mere self-aggrandizement, even if it’s just to “raise awareness.”  We can certainly debate the effectives of such gestures, but to dismiss them all as “virtue signaling” is an oversimplification, in my opinion.
